candidates.text: Hypothesis: the storage path's constant recorded value collapses token entropy, because the lookup returns the stored value, not the key it looked up, and the handler re-uses that value as the validated token; validation therefore accepts a fixed constant that any attacker knows in advance. Prerequisites: default non-single-use configuration with the memory backend, disposable in-process app, fake request interface. Bounded test: first safe request mints a random cookie; replay it on a second safe request and read the rotated cookie value; then send a state-changing request from a completely fresh client with the suspected constant as both the extracted token and the cookie, plus a control state-changing request with an attacker-chosen unknown random value. Expected support: the second safe response rotates the cookie to the constant and the fresh-client constant request is accepted (success status) while the unknown value is rejected. Falsifier: the constant request is rejected or the cookie never collapses. Cleanup: fixtures are disposable; keep the sequence script as the regression core.

Hypothesis: token rotation fails because the new token equals the previous constant value, creating a standing replay window visible on safe methods alone. Prerequisites: non-single-use mode, disposable app fixture. Bounded test: issue three sequential safe requests in one client session, logging the cookie value each time. Expected support: after the first repeat the cookie stays the fixed constant indefinitely. Falsifier: cookie values vary across requests. Limitation: cookie collapse alone does not prove a state-changing request is accepted, so pair with an unsafe-method check. Cleanup: discard fixtures.

Hypothesis: accepted tokens are not bound to any client session at all, so a token observed from one client validates from a different client. Prerequisites: two independent client sessions against one disposable app instance. Bounded test: obtain a cookie pair from client A, then submit a state-changing request from client B using the same values. Expected support: client B's request is accepted. Falsifier: it is rejected. Limitation: with the constant-collapse mechanism this tests binding rather than predictability; most informative after the primary bypass is shown. Cleanup: reset stores between clients.

Hypothesis (control): constant-value predictability, not storage indirection itself, is necessary for trivial exploitation. Prerequisites: a configurable fake storage backend that can return distinct random values. Bounded test: drive the same request sequence against a backend returning distinct random values per key and compare acceptance behavior with the constant-value backend. Expected support: only the constant backend accepts the attacker-known value. Falsifier: the random-value backend also accepts it, which would indicate a second defect beyond entropy loss. Limitation: an elaborate control for the first step; better used as a robustness ingredient after the primary mechanism is confirmed. Cleanup: remove the fake backend.
